key_terms.meaning: The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment; each run of the experiment gives exactly one point of S.
A subset A of the sample space; P(A) is a number attached to that subset.
(i) P(A) ≥ 0, (ii) P(S) = 1, (iii) for disjoint A₁, A₂, … , P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ …) = Σ P(Aᵢ).
P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), with P(B) > 0; the sample space is reduced to B.
A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), which makes P(A|B) = P(A).
A set of events B₁, B₂, … that are disjoint and together fill S, so one and only one of them occurs.
For a partition {Bᵢ}, P(A) = Σᵢ P(A|Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ); the event A is broken into weighted cases.
P(Bᵢ|A) = P(A|Bᵢ) P(Bᵢ) / Σⱼ P(A|Bⱼ) P(Bⱼ); it reverses which event is conditioned on.
A function X: S → ℝ that assigns a real number to every outcome.
For a discrete X, p(x) = P(X = x), with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σ p(x) = 1.
For a continuous X, f(x) ≥ 0 with P(a < X ≤ b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx and total integral 1.
F(x) = P(X ≤ x); it rises from 0 to 1, never decreases, and is right-continuous.
The long-run weighted average: Σ x p(x) for discrete X, ∫ x f(x) dx for continuous X.
Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ², where μ = E[X]; it measures spread about the mean.
Raw moment μ′ᵣ = E[Xʳ]; central moment μᵣ = E[(X − μ)ʳ]. μ₁′ = μ, μ₂ = Var(X).
M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}], defined for t near 0; its derivatives at t = 0 give the moments.
P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k² for any k > 0, using only the mean μ and standard deviation σ.
Y = g(X) is a new RV; its pdf comes from f_Y(y) = Σ f_X(xᵢ) / |g′(xᵢ)| over all roots xᵢ of g(xᵢ) = y.
The set of values x where the pmf is non-zero or the pdf is positive; outside it the probability is 0.

takeaways: Probability is a set function obeying three axioms, so every rule you use later is a consequence of those axioms, not a separate assumption.
Conditioning shrinks the sample space to B and rescales all probabilities by 1/P(B); independence is exactly the case where this rescaling changes nothing.
The law of total probability breaks an event into cases over a partition, and Bayes' theorem runs the same arithmetic backwards to turn P(A|B) into P(B|A).
A random variable converts outcomes into numbers, and the pmf, pdf or CDF then carries all the probability information in a form you can compute with.
Expectation is a weighted average and variance is the average squared gap from it; both are linear-friendly tools, with Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X).
The MGF packages all moments into one function, so a single differentiation gives E[X], a double differentiation gives E[X²], and matching MGFs proves two distributions are the same.
Chebyshev's inequality gives a worst-case bound from only μ and σ, useful when the exact distribution is unknown, though it is usually loose.
When Y = g(X), the density is not simply g(f_X(x)); you must transform the variable, use the Jacobian |dx/dy|, and add a term for every pre-image of y.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always pair a short axiomatic/definitional part with a full numerical problem, most often a Bayes' theorem question on machines, urns or quality control, plus a derivation of moments or an MGF for a standard distribution.

bank.q: State the three axioms of probability. Using only these axioms, prove that (i) P(A<sup>c</sup>) = 1 − P(A) and (ii) P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
outline: Write Kolmogorov's three axioms with P(A) ≥ 0, P(S) = 1 and countable additivity for disjoint events.
For (i): S = A ∪ A<sup>c</sup> with A, A<sup>c</sup> disjoint, so 1 = P(A) + P(A<sup>c</sup>).
For (ii): split A ∪ B into A and B ∩ A<sup>c</sup>, and B into A ∩ B and B ∩ A<sup>c</sup>.
Subtract to get the addition rule; mention it reduces to P(A) + P(B) when A and B are disjoint.

bank.q: Define conditional probability. Show that P(A ∩ B) = P(A|B)P(B), extend this to three events, and state the condition for A and B to be independent.
outline: Definition P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) with P(B) > 0, and the reason P(B) must be non-zero.
Multiplication rule for two events and the chain rule P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A)P(B|A)P(C|A ∩ B).
Independence as P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), equivalent to P(A|B) = P(A).
Warn that pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.

bank.q: State and prove the law of total probability for a partition of the sample space, and use it to state Bayes' theorem.
outline: Define a partition: events Bᵢ disjoint with union S.
Write A as the disjoint union of A ∩ Bᵢ.
Apply additivity and the multiplication rule to get P(A) = Σ P(A|Bᵢ)P(Bᵢ).
Substitute into the definition of P(Bᵢ|A) to obtain Bayes' theorem; name prior, likelihood and posterior.

bank.q: Define a random variable, a discrete random variable and a continuous random variable. Give the properties of the distribution function F(x) and state how F is obtained from a pmf and from a pdf.
outline: Random variable as a real-valued function on the sample space.
Discrete: countable support, pmf p(x) with p(x) ≥ 0 and Σp(x) = 1; continuous: pdf f(x) ≥ 0 with total integral 1.
F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = Σ over xᵢ ≤ x of p(xᵢ), or ∫ from −∞ to x of f(t) dt.
Properties: 0 ≤ F ≤ 1, non-decreasing, right-continuous, F(−∞) = 0, F(∞) = 1.
For continuous X, f(x) = F′(x) and P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a).

bank.q: Two machines M₁ and M₂ make 60% and 40% of a factory's output. Their defective rates are 2% and 5%. A finished item drawn at random is found defective. Find the probability it came from M₂. Also find the overall defective rate.
outline: Define the partition {M₁, M₂} and the event D = defective.
Write the priors P(M₁) = 0.60, P(M₂) = 0.40 and likelihoods P(D|M₁) = 0.02, P(D|M₂) = 0.05.
State the posterior for M₁ as a check that the two posteriors sum to 1.

bank.q: A continuous random variable X has pdf f(x) = c x² for 0 < x < 1 and 0 elsewhere. Find c, the CDF, P(0.2 < X < 0.6), E[X] and Var(X).
outline: Normalise: ∫₀¹ c x² dx = c/3 = 1, so c = 3.
F(x) = 0 for x ≤ 0, x³ for 0 < x < 1, 1 for x ≥ 1.
E[X] = ∫ 3x³ dx from 0 to 1 = 3/4; E[X²] = 3/5.

bank.q: Derive the moment generating function of the binomial distribution B(n, p) and use it to obtain the mean and the variance.
outline: M_X(t) = Σ from x = 0 to n of e<sup>tx</sup> C(n,x) p<sup>x</sup> q<sup>n−x</sup>.
Collect terms to get (q + p e<sup>t</sup>)<sup>n</sup>.
M′_X(t) = n p e<sup>t</sup>(q + p e<sup>t</sup>)<sup>n−1</sup>; at t = 0 this gives np.
M″_X(0) = n(n − 1)p² + np.

bank.q: X is uniform on (−1, 1). Find the pdf of Y = X². Explain why two pre-images of y must be counted.
outline: f_X(x) = 1/2 on (−1, 1), 0 elsewhere.
For 0 < y < 1 the equation x² = y has roots x₁ = √y and x₂ = −√y.
Apply f_Y(y) = Σ f_X(xᵢ)/|g′(xᵢ)| with g′(x) = 2x, so |g′(xᵢ)| = 2√y for both roots.
Note the density blows up near 0 but still integrates to 1; Y is not uniform.

bank.q: State Chebyshev's inequality. Using it, find how many times a fair coin must be tossed so that the proportion of heads lies within 0.05 of 1/2 with probability at least 0.9.
outline: State P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k², or the form P(|X − μ| < ε) ≥ 1 − σ²/ε².
For n tosses, X = heads, μ = n/2, σ² = n/4.
Set ε = 0.05n, require n/4 ≤ 0.1(0.05n)².
Comment that the bound is far larger than the true requirement, so Chebyshev is conservative.

bank.q: The number of calls arriving at a helpline in a minute is Poisson with mean 3. Using the MGF, find E[X] and Var(X), and then estimate P(X ≥ 8) using Chebyshev's inequality.
outline: M_X(t) = exp(3(e<sup>t</sup> − 1)).
σ = √3 ≈ 1.732; take k = (8 − 3)/√3 ≈ 2.89 in a one-sided reading of the bound.
Chebyshev gives P(|X − 3| ≥ 5) ≤ 3/25 = 0.12, so P(X ≥ 8) ≤ 0.12.
Note the true Poisson tail is roughly 0.012, so the bound is valid but very loose.

bank.q: In a test for a disease present in 1 in 1000 people, the test detects the disease 99% of the time and gives a false positive 2% of the time. A person tests positive. Find the probability the person actually has the disease and discuss why the answer is so small.
outline: Partition {D, D<sup>c</sup>} with P(D) = 0.001, P(D<sup>c</sup>) = 0.999.
Likelihoods P(+|D) = 0.99, P(+|D<sup>c</sup>) = 0.02.
Discuss the dominance of the false positives because the prior is tiny; a repeat test raises the posterior sharply.

bank.q: Explain why the MGF may fail to exist for some distributions while moments still exist, and how the characteristic function removes the problem. Show how moments are extracted from an MGF that exists.
outline: M_X(t) = E[e<sup>tX</sup>] requires the expectation to be finite for t in some open interval around 0.
Give a heavy-tailed example such as the Cauchy or log-normal where the integral diverges for every t ≠ 0.
Expansion M_X(t) = Σ μ′ᵣ t<sup>r</sup>/r! shows μ′ᵣ as r! times the coefficient of t<sup>r</sup>.
Differentiate r times at t = 0: M<sup>(r)</sup>_X(0) = E[X<sup>r</sup>].
Characteristic function φ_X(t) = E[e<sup>itX</sup>] is bounded by 1 in modulus, so it always exists and serves the same purpose.

bank.q: Two independent random variables X and Y both follow the standard uniform distribution on (0, 1). Find the pdf of U = X + Y by the CDF (convolution) method and verify that the total area is 1.
outline: Write F_U(u) = P(X + Y ≤ u) as the area of the region inside the unit square below x + y = u.
For 0 ≤ u ≤ 1 the area is u²/2; for 1 < u ≤ 2 it is 1 − (2 − u)²/2.
Differentiate to get f_U(u) = u on (0, 1) and 2 − u on (1, 2).
Check symmetry about u = 1 and that the two triangles each have area 1/2.
State that this is the triangular distribution and note the general convolution formula.

bank.q: A random variable X has mean 50 and standard deviation 5 but an unknown distribution. Compare the information Markov's inequality and Chebyshev's inequality give for P(X ≥ 70), and comment on which bound an engineer should quote.
outline: Markov applied to the non-negative variable (X − 50)²: P((X − 50)² ≥ 400) ≤ 25/400, the same number; explain the link.
Markov on X itself needs X ≥ 0 and gives P(X ≥ 70) ≤ 50/70 ≈ 0.714, much weaker.
State that both are distribution-free and therefore conservative.
Conclude that Chebyshev is the sharper usable bound here; with a known distribution, use the exact tail.

bank.q: Let Y = g(X) for a strictly increasing g. Derive the density of Y from the CDF, then extend the result to a non-monotone g. Explain the role of the Jacobian and of multiplicity.
outline: Start from F_Y(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y) = P(X ≤ g<sup>−1</sup>(y)) = F_X(g<sup>−1</sup>(y)).
Differentiate using the chain rule: f_Y(y) = f_X(x)|dx/dy| with x = g<sup>−1</sup>(y).
Identify |dx/dy| = 1/|g′(x)| as the one-dimensional Jacobian.
For non-monotone g, sum over all roots: f_Y(y) = Σ f_X(xᵢ)/|g′(xᵢ)|.
Explain that the Jacobian corrects for the stretching of the x-axis, and that summing counts each pre-image exactly once.

glossary.def: A procedure whose outcome cannot be predicted with certainty but whose set of possible outcomes is known.
The set S of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.
A single result of one run of the experiment; one element of S.
A subset of the sample space, to which a probability is assigned.
Events that cannot occur together, so their intersection is empty and their probabilities add.
A collection of events whose union is the whole sample space.
The event A<sup>c</sup> that A does not occur; P(A<sup>c</sup>) = 1 − P(A).
A sample space in which every outcome has the same probability, giving P(A) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B), the probability of A once B is known to have occurred.
Events satisfying P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); knowing one occurred gives no information about the other.
A collection of pairwise disjoint events whose union is the sample space.
The probability P(Bᵢ) of a case before any evidence about event A is used.
The updated probability P(Bᵢ|A) computed by Bayes' theorem after the evidence A is observed.
The conditional probability P(A|Bᵢ) of the observed evidence under a particular case.
A real-valued function defined on the sample space.
A random variable whose set of possible values is finite or countably infinite.
A random variable whose CDF is a continuous function, described by a density.
The function p(x) = P(X = x) for a discrete random variable.
A non-negative function f whose integral over an interval gives the probability that X lies in that interval.
F(x) = P(X ≤ x), valid for both discrete and continuous random variables.
The probability-weighted average of the values of a random variable, written E[X] or μ.
The expected squared deviation from the mean, Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])².
The square root of the variance, in the same units as X.
μ′ᵣ = E[X<sup>r</sup>], the r-th moment about the origin.
μᵣ = E[(X − μ)<sup>r</sup>], the r-th moment about the mean; μ₂ is the variance.
M_X(t) = E[e<sup>tX</sup>], whose derivatives at t = 0 give the raw moments.
The factor |dx/dy| (or its multivariate determinant) that corrects for the stretching of scale in a change of variable.
